claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in high-entropy FCC/BCC multilayers under sustained loading is governed by stress-induced formation and evolution of nanoscale twin networks at layer interfaces.
Interfacial twin networks mediate dislocation motion and accommodate plastic strain.
Twin-network activity can balance strength and deformation tolerance.
The proposed initial material has distinct nanoscale FCC and BCC layers.
The proposed initial material has well-defined coherent interfaces and minimal pre-existing twins.
Elevated-temperature sustained mechanical loading stimulates plastic deformation in the multilayer.
The relevant structural mediator consists of interfacial nanoscale twin networks combined with localized dislocation activity.
Partial-dislocation motion nucleates and grows twin boundaries at the interfaces.
The resulting twins accommodate plastic deformation and interact with lattice distortions inherent to high-entropy alloys.
Twin–lattice-distortion interactions modulate creep through competing strengthening and softening effects.
Sustained loading will cause progressive formation and widening of interfacial twin networks.
Sustained loading will increase interfacial dislocation density.
Sustained loading will produce a measurable increase in creep strain relative to baseline.
The mechanism applies only while the nanoscale multilayer architecture is retained.
The mechanism requires a temperature and loading-rate regime that permits dislocation-mediated twinning without complete homogenization or phase transformation.
A lack of significant correlation between twin-network formation or interfacial dislocation-density changes and increased creep strain would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
